entries.topic: Non-identification and its end: Israel between East and West, 1948–1951 (the PRC recognition and the Korean War vote)

sources.label: Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", International Journal of Middle East Studies 36:4 (November 2004), pp. 657–673
Hillel Kuttler, "Between Seoul and Jerusalem", National Library of Israel blog (2026)
"Interview with Prof. Yitzhak Shichor: American Interests Affect the Changes in Israel-China Relations", INSS
Visits by Foreign Leaders, 1951, Office of the Historian, US Department of State

claims.text: On 27 September 1948 Ben-Gurion told the Provisional State Council: "We do not want to subordinate ourselves to anyone, and we do not believe that angels rule anywhere."

The Basic Principles of the Government Programme of 9 March 1949 made friendship with both superpowers the first principle of foreign policy, referring to "friendship with all freedom-loving states, and in particular with the United States and the Soviet Union."

The policy was called non-identification (i-hizdahut). The diplomat Michael Comay summarized it: "To try to retain the support of both, we adopted a posture of non-identification, of keeping out of the Cold War." Moshe Sharett, its main advocate, urged "knocking on every door". Shlaim reads it as a pragmatic policy of national interest rather than an ideological neutrality.

On 9 January 1950 Israel recognized the People's Republic of China, the first country in the Middle East and the seventh in the non-communist world to do so. Formal diplomatic relations followed only on 24 January 1992.

According to Soviet documents cited by Yitzhak Shichor, Zhou Enlai told the Soviet ambassador in July 1951 that China would not establish diplomatic relations with Israel; Shichor also says Washington, with the Korean War in the background, urged Israel not to forge relations with Beijing, "even using threats", and identifies the United States as the main factor keeping the two apart.

Israel's cabinet first discussed participation in the UN coalition in Korea on 2 July 1950, at President Weizmann's home in Rehovot, eight days after the war began; the statement reported on 7 July read: "The Israel government opposes and condemns aggression whenever it occurs and from whatever quarter it emanates."

On 4 July 1950 Ben-Gurion told the Knesset that Israel's vote for the UN resolution condemning North Korea was "a vote for the United Nations and for the principles it embodied", and rejected calls to abstain. Israel offered no troops. Shlaim calls the vote "the decisive break at the declaratory level with the policy of non-identification."

Israel sent $100,000 worth of food and medicine for Korea, was appointed to the 14-member Peace Observation Commission (never sent to the peninsula), and drafted a seven-point peace plan whose sponsorship passed to Norway; the communist party Maki advocated support for North Korea.

In late July 1950 Ben-Gurion told the US ambassador he planned an army of 250,000 built with American help, "capable and anxious" to aid the United States, Britain and Turkey against Soviet aggression; the ambassador reported that the prime minister "could not have been more explicit about his desire to commit Israel unreservedly to the West."

Interpretation: Michael Brecher (quoted by Shlaim) held that the shift was "catalyzed by the need for arms and economic aid"; Shlaim adds three reasons: the fall in immigration from Eastern Europe, the aim of winning American Jewry, and the need for US backing for German reparations. Shlaim: "The tilt towards the West was probably inevitable from the start, but it occurred in a surprisingly sudden manner."

Ben-Gurion's first visit to the United States as prime minister is listed by the State Department as a goodwill visit, 3–8 May 1951, that also promoted Israel Bonds, with stops in Knoxville, New York, West Point, Philadelphia, Princeton, Baltimore, Boston, Pittsburgh, Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland and Los Angeles; the same entry says he left the United States on 31 May.

disputes.question: Why did Israel abandon non-identification in 1950?

positions.view: It was catalyzed by Israel's need for arms and economic aid (Brecher), with the decline of East European immigration, the courting of American Jewry and the need for US backing on German reparations as further reasons (Shlaim).

The Israeli establishment held that the rift with Moscow followed the Soviet Union's own 'developmental logic' (Sharett's phrase), so Israel was pushed rather than chose; Shlaim, citing Uri Bialer, challenges this as too deterministic.

entries.topic: The Tripartite Declaration of 25 May 1950 and Western arms policy

sources.label: Tripartite Declaration Regarding the Armistice Borders, 25 May 1950 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
Tripartite Declaration: statement by the Governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and France, 25 May 1950 (UNISPAL, non-UN document)
FRUS 1950, vol. V, doc. 78: First Progress Report on NSC 65/3, 'United States Policy toward Arms Shipments to the Near East', 7 August 1950
FRUS 1950, vol. V, doc. 495: Memorandum of conversation, 'Tripartite Declaration of May 25, 1950' (Malik, Hare), June 1950
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", International Journal of Middle East Studies 36:4 (November 2004), pp. 657–673

claims.text: The United States, Britain and France issued the declaration on 25 May 1950, after the Foreign Ministers' meeting in London (tripartite communiqué of 13 May 1950); it was printed in the Department of State Bulletin of 5 June 1950, p. 886.

Paragraph 1 accepted that the Arab states and Israel needed armed forces for internal security and self-defence, reaffirmed the three governments' opposition (stated at the Security Council on 4 August 1949) to an arms race between them, and said: "All applications for arms or war material for these countries will be considered in the light of these principles."

Paragraph 2 recorded that recipient states had given assurances that the purchasing state "does not intend to undertake any act of aggression against any other state", and said similar assurances would be sought from future recipients.

Paragraph 3 declared the three governments' "unalterable opposition to the use of force or threat of force" between states in the area and pledged that, if any state were preparing to violate frontiers or armistice lines, they would act immediately, within and outside the United Nations, to prevent it.

NSC 65/3 was approved as policy on 19 May 1950; the Under Secretary of State's progress report of 7 August 1950 says the declaration was drafted at the London meeting in line with it, and that US policy allowed only equipment needed "to help the states there to maintain internal order and provide for legitimate defense" while seeking to "avoid being drawn into any arms race in the area."

The same report records Arab press criticism that the declaration "froze" the territorial status quo, a generally favourable joint commentary from the Council of the Arab League on 12 June 1950, and says Israel welcomed it as recognizing Israel as "a permanent element in the Near East."

When Lebanon's minister Charles Malik asked for clarification in June 1950, the State Department's Raymond Hare told him "There was, of course, no intent to recognize spheres of influence" and that the declaration's wording "should not be given a legalistic interpretation"; Malik called it potentially the three powers' most important contribution to peace if implemented with "honest and sustained impartiality."
Shlaim writes that Israel had rejected the declaration as unfavourable; Ben-Gurion's diary of 30 May 1950 accused it of permitting arms to the Arab states while denying them to Israel.

disputes.question: How did Israel receive the Tripartite Declaration?

positions.view: Israel was pleased and welcomed it as recognizing Israel as 'a permanent element in the Near East' (US Under Secretary of State's report to the NSC, 7 August 1950).
Israel rejected it as unfavourable; Ben-Gurion's diary of 30 May 1950 accused it of arming the Arab states while denying arms to Israel (Shlaim).

entries.topic: The first US grant aid to Israel: the $150 million request and the Mutual Security Acts of 1951 and 1952

sources.label: FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 297: Memorandum of conversation, Acheson with Ambassador Eban and David Horowitz (March 1951)
FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 24: Editorial note on McGhee's memorandum of 17 April 1951 on Near East economic aid
FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 417: McGhee to the Secretary of State, 'Visit of Mr. Abraham Feinberg, at the Suggestion of the President' (July 1951)
JTA, "Senate and House get bills calling for U.S. to grant Israel $150,000,000 in aid", 3 April 1951
I. L. Kenen to Abba Hillel Silver, letter from Washington, 1951 (Abba Hillel Silver Papers, MS-4787, American Jewish Archives)
Truman, letter to committee chairmen on financing the UN Palestine refugee program, 27 July 1951 (Public Papers, Truman Library)
JTA, "Congress asked to vote $76,000,000 for Israel refugee aid", 14 March 1952
JTA, "House-Senate conference agrees on $70,000,000 for Israel aid", 5 June 1952
JTA, "House approves mutual security aid to Israel", 6 June 1952
JTA, "AIPAC founder I. L. Kenen dead at 83" (1988)
Eldad Beck, "The deal that disappeared", Israel Hayom, 19 October 2018 (on research by Kobby Barda)

claims.text: In March 1951 Ambassador Abba Eban and David Horowitz of Israel's Finance Ministry handed Acheson a note requesting a $150 million grant-in-aid for 1 July 1951 to 1 June 1952, citing population growth (510,000 since statehood, 600,000 more expected over three years), defence spending and commitments to the UNRWA reintegration fund; they also asked US support for a $1.5 billion reparations claim on Germany. Acheson said an official invitation for Ben-Gurion was impossible that year.

An editorial note in FRUS records that the request for a fiscal year 1952 grant of $150 million "had generated a great deal of discussion within the United States Government", prompting McGhee's memorandum of 17 April 1951 proposing a program of economic aid to the Near East.

On about 3 April 1951 Senators Paul Douglas (Democrat, Illinois) and Robert Taft (Republican, Ohio) introduced a bill for $150 million in aid to Israel, with a House bill from Majority Leader John McCormack; the senators called Israel "a bulwark in that area of world democracy" against Communist threats, "particularly in Iran", and McCormack called it "a dependable ally of the United States."

The Administration's recommendation to Congress on 24 May 1951 was $23.5 million in economic aid for Israel, $23.5 million for the Arab states, $50 million for the Arab refugee program and authority for $41.5 million in direct military grants; McGhee declined Jacob Blaustein's request for $75 million each and proposed telling Abraham Feinberg that the $50 million for Arab refugees could be seen as indirect aid to Israel. The memorandum lists $135 million in earlier Export-Import Bank credit to Israel.

I. L. Kenen's letter to Abba Hillel Silver describes the Senate fight of August 1951: a Douglas amendment, backed by Taft, raised the Near East economic aid figure and Israel's total to about $68.8 million (the scan is partly illegible), passed on a close standing vote; Kenen stressed that "all this is still an authorization." He contrasted Israel's share of about 1% in the Administration bill with about 5.2% in the Senate bill.

Truman's letter of 27 July 1951 records a US contribution of $25,450,000 to the UN Palestine refugee program in fiscal 1951 and a request of $50,000,000 in the Mutual Security Program; he signed the Mutual Security Act of 1951 on 10 October 1951, which provided $50 million for the UN program in fiscal 1952.
According to Kenen's JTA obituary, the 1951 campaign sought $150 million for Israel and, despite State Department opposition, Kenen won approval for $65 million.

For fiscal 1953 the Administration asked in March 1952 for $76 million for the relief and resettlement of Jewish immigrants in Israel and $65 million for the UN to resettle Arab refugees in Arab lands, $141 million of a $196 million Near East request; Acheson and W. Averell Harriman testified for it.

In June 1952 a House–Senate conference set Israel's figure at $70,228,000 for relief and rehabilitation of Jewish refugees plus $2,772,000 in technical assistance, splitting the difference between the House ($76 million) and the Senate ($64,456,000); Congress cut the Administration's overall aid by about 20% but Israel's by less than 8%.

Kobby Barda's research, as reported by Israel Hayom, describes the refugee-aid design as $50 million each for Israel and the Arab states for refugee absorption, with a further $53 million for Arab states in technical cooperation, and the $50 million for Arab refugees channelled through UNRWA.

disputes.question: How much did Congress grant Israel for fiscal 1952?

positions.view: $65 million, against a goal of $150 million (Kenen's JTA obituary).
About $68.8 million at the Senate authorization stage, after the Douglas amendment (Kenen's own 1951 letter, partly illegible, which stresses that this was still only an authorization).

entries.topic: Kenen, the aid campaign and the lobby's founding in its Cold War frame (1950–1954), with American Jewish dissent

sources.label: JTA, "AIPAC founder I. L. Kenen dead at 83" (1988)
American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Jewish Virtual Library
Eldad Beck, "The deal that disappeared", Israel Hayom, 19 October 2018 (on research by Kobby Barda)
I. L. Kenen to Abba Hillel Silver, letter from Washington, 1951 (Abba Hillel Silver Papers, MS-4787, American Jewish Archives)
Mark K. Bauman, "The Blaustein–Ben-Gurion Agreement", Jewish Museum of Maryland (from Generations 2007–2008)
American Council for Judaism, Encyclopaedia Judaica (2nd ed., 2007) via Jewish Virtual Library

claims.text: I. L. Kenen directed the American Emergency Committee on Zionist Affairs' lobbying from 1943, was the Jewish Agency's information director at the UN in 1947–48, and was a member of Israel's first delegation to the UN in 1949.

According to Israel Hayom's account of Kobby Barda's research, Abba Eban, then Israel's ambassador to the UN, suggested that Kenen go to Washington, and Kenen argued that the best route to aid was to extend the Marshall Plan approach to the Middle East within a broader refugee framework.

Kenen's 1951 letter to Abba Hillel Silver, written from Washington, reports the Senate floor work on the aid amendment and names Senators Douglas, Taft and Brewster and the lobbyist Julius Klein among those involved.

Kenen's JTA obituary says he moved to Washington in 1951 and set up the American Zionist Committee "to lobby Congress in support of Israel", that the committee became AIPAC in 1954, and that in 1957 he used a $700 speaking honorarium to start the weekly Near East Report.

The Jewish Virtual Library dates AIPAC's beginnings to 1951 within the American Zionist Council, says the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs was set up as a separate lobbying entity in 1954 because the Council's non-profit status limited its lobbying, and dates the name American Israel Public Affairs Committee to 1959.

On 23 August 1950, at a luncheon in Jerusalem, Ben-Gurion and the American Jewish Committee's Jacob Blaustein exchanged statements in which Israel recognized American Jews' allegiance to the United States and each side undertook not to speak on behalf of the other.

The American Council for Judaism, whose first president was Lessing Rosenwald and whose chief spokesman was Elmer Berger, had opposed the establishment of Israel and remained critical of "the Israel-Zionist domination of American Jewish life"; it claimed 20,000 members and by the end of 1955 had set up ten schools teaching classical Reform positions.

disputes.question: When was the pro-Israel congressional lobby founded, and under what name?

positions.view: In 1951, when Kenen set up the American Zionist Committee in Washington; it became AIPAC in 1954 (Kenen's JTA obituary).

It began in 1951 inside the American Zionist Council; the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs was created as a separate lobbying body in 1954 and took the name AIPAC in 1959 (Jewish Virtual Library).

entries.topic: Founding Israel's intelligence community: Aman, the Shin Bet and the Mossad (1948–1952)

sources.label: The Israeli Security Agency (ISA/Shin Bet/Shabak), Jewish Virtual Library
Prime Minister Ben-Gurion's secret directive establishing the coordinating institute (the Mossad), 13 December 1949 (text, Jewish Virtual Library)
Reuven Shiloah (Zaslani), Encyclopaedia Judaica (2007) via Jewish Virtual Library
Mossad leaders, GlobalSecurity.org
The establishment of the Institute for Intelligence and Special Operations (Mossad): history and heads, mossad.gov.il

claims.text: On 30 June 1948, a month after the IDF was established, the Haganah Intelligence Service was dissolved and three services took its place: military intelligence (Aman), the Foreign Ministry's Political Division for operations abroad, and an internal security service under Isser Harel that became the Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet).

The Jewish Virtual Library states that the Security Service's existence was anchored in law on 18 February 1949, that its existence was not made public until 1957, and that a statute defining its responsibilities was passed only in February 2002.

A secret directive from the Prime Minister to the Foreign Ministry dated 13 December 1949 stated that "an institute is being established to co-ordinate state intelligence agencies"; Reuven Shiloah, the Foreign Ministry's adviser for special projects, was to organize and head it, reporting to the Prime Minister, with his office inside the Foreign Ministry for administrative purposes.
The directive asked for about IL20,000 for 1950–51, of which IL5,000 was for special operations requiring the Prime Minister's prior authorization.

Shiloah had formed the state's political intelligence service in 1948 and taken part in the Rhodes and Lausanne talks of 1949; on 2 March 1951 Ben-Gurion ordered him to set up a 'Directorate' to take all overseas intelligence operations under its wing; he retired in 1952, was replaced by Isser Harel, and served as minister at Israel's Washington embassy in 1953–57.

GlobalSecurity.org records the body's earlier names (Central Institute for Coordination, later Central Institute for Intelligence and Security), says bureaucratic conflict delayed its becoming fully operational for more than a year, dates a reorganization to 1 April 1951, notes the exposure of an Israeli spy ring in Baghdad in 1951, and says Ben-Gurion made Harel, the 'Memuneh', responsible for both the Mossad and the Shin Bet.
The Mossad's own list of heads gives Reuven Shiloah for 1949–1952 and Isser Harel for 1952–1963.

entries.topic: The origins of CIA–Israeli intelligence liaison (1951 and after)

sources.label: Yossi Melman and Dan Raviv, "Spies Like Us", Tablet, 8 April 2010
David Robarge, "'Cunning Passages, Contrived Corridors': Wandering in the Angletonian Wilderness", Studies in Intelligence 53:4 (2009), CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
Jeff McConnell, "Israeli Spies in the US", MERIP, January 1986
Reuven Shiloah (Zaslani), Encyclopaedia Judaica (2007) via Jewish Virtual Library

claims.text: Melman and Raviv write that in 1948 the CIA initially viewed the new state as part of the Soviet sphere of influence.

In 1951 Ben-Gurion, touring the United States, met General Walter Bedell Smith, Truman's Director of Central Intelligence, and "convinced U.S. intelligence to give Israel a try"; the account describes no formal agreement or terms.

After that visit, according to Melman and Raviv, James Jesus Angleton "was put in charge of the U.S. side", with Amos Manor and Teddy Kollek as his Israeli counterparts; Manor later said: "It wasn't easy to persuade the anti-communist Angleton that we could be friends."
The Encyclopaedia Judaica says Reuven Shiloah developed contacts with the CIA and other Western intelligence services, without giving a date.

The CIA's own historian David Robarge writes that Angleton became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, that his control of Israel's account at the CIA was "an administrative anomaly" and one of the foundations of his influence, and that he saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union.

Jeff McConnell (MERIP, 1986) wrote that Angleton had exercised formal authority over CIA liaison with Israel "since the early 1950s (how early is a matter of dispute)", that the Israel desk sat under his counterintelligence staff, and that a deliberate effort to end covert operations against each other came in the mid-1950s; he cites Wolf Blitzer for a "discreet arrangement since the 1950s, banning covert operations against each other."
Melman and Raviv call the 1956 handover to the CIA, via Israeli intelligence in Warsaw, of Khrushchev's secret speech "the great turning point" of the relationship.

disputes.question: When did a formal CIA–Israeli liaison, and a no-spying understanding, begin, and when did Angleton take charge?

positions.view: The relationship began after Ben-Gurion's 1951 visit and meeting with Bedell Smith, with Angleton then put in charge of the US side (Melman and Raviv).

How early Angleton held authority is disputed; the effort to stop covert operations against each other dates to the mid-1950s (McConnell, citing Blitzer); Angleton headed the Counterintelligence Staff only from 1954 (Robarge).

entries.topic: The Huleh drainage crisis on the Syrian front and Security Council Resolution 93 (March–July 1951)

sources.label: Security Council Resolution 93 (1951), 18 May 1951 (UNISPAL)
Yearbook of the United Nations 1951–52, 'The Palestine Question' (excerpts, UNISPAL)
Statement to the Security Council by Ambassador Eban, 18 May 1951 (text, Jewish Virtual Library)

claims.text: Between 29 March and 6 April 1951 Syria complained (S/2061, S/2065, S/2074) that Israel was violating the July 1949 armistice by draining and deepening the Jordan riverbed, occupying the demilitarized zone, firing on Syrian posts, forcibly evacuating Arab inhabitants and demolishing their villages, and bombing El Hamma and Syrian outposts.

Syria argued that drainage would give Israel a military advantage, create more refugees, require new Syrian outposts and impair irrigation, and that it should have been consulted because most of the zone had been under Syrian occupation; the Arab landowners, Syria said, were protecting their land from expropriation.

Israel (S/2072) said the drainage had gone on since October 1950 with Syrian and UN knowledge, that Syrian forces entered El Hamma on 4 April 1951 and attacked a police patrol, killing seven policemen and seriously wounding three, that the work was lawful and needed no Syrian consent, and asserted sovereignty over the zone; its air action of 5 April was described as a response.

Resolution 93 of 18 May 1951 found that "Aerial action taken by the forces of the Government of Israel on 5 April 1951" violated the cease-fire of resolution 54 (1948), endorsed the requests that the Palestine Land Development Company be told "to cease all operations in the demilitarized zone" until agreement, and decided that Arab civilians removed from the zone "should be permitted to return forthwith to their homes" under Mixed Armistice Commission supervision.
Resolution 93 was adopted at the 547th meeting by 10 votes to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining.

The UN Chief of Staff's memorandum of June 1951 concluded that neither party held sovereignty in the demilitarized zone and that the work should stop until Israel and Syria agreed; he reported that the Arab landowners rejected any proposal to rent, sell or exchange their land.
On 8 July 1951 the Chief of Staff reported that 785 civilians had been evacuated from the zone; the Mixed Armistice Commission chairman interviewed 632 of them, and about 260 chose to return.

Israel complained on 7 May 1951 (S/2126) of an attack by Syrian irregulars on Tel el Mutilla inside Israel; a UN report (S/2359, 23 September 1951) said the allegation of Syrian army participation "could now be considered as having been proved", citing medal awards in the Syrian Official Gazette. Syria denied army involvement (S/2360).

Eban told the Council on 18 May 1951 that the draft "does confer a veto power upon the very interests which are implacably opposed" to drainage, that the project would reclaim "10,000 acres from desolation and 25,000 acres from disease", objected that Israel's 5 April action was censured while Syrian attacks were not, and said whoever holds the Huleh area "clutches Israel at its throat."

disputes.question: Who held sovereignty in the Israeli–Syrian demilitarized zone?

positions.view: Israel asserted sovereignty over the zone and held that civilian work there needed no Syrian consent.
Syria said it should have been consulted, most of the zone having been under Syrian occupation; the UN Chief of Staff found that neither party held sovereignty in the zone.

entries.topic: Egypt's Suez Canal restrictions on Israel-bound shipping and Security Council Resolution 95 (1 September 1951)

sources.label: Resolution adopted by the UN Security Council on 1 September 1951 (FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 477)
UN Security Council, 558th meeting (S/PV.558), 1 September 1951, record
UN Security Council, 553rd meeting (S/PV.553), 16 August 1951, record
Leo Gross, "Passage Through the Suez Canal of Israel-Bound Cargo and Israel Ships", American Journal of International Law 51:3 (1957), pp. 530–568

claims.text: The resolution of 1 September 1951 noted that the armistice regime had lasted nearly two and a half years and was "of a permanent character", and that Egypt had not heeded the Chief of Staff's plea to stop "interfering with the passage through the Suez Canal of goods destined for Israel."

It found the practice "an abuse of the exercise of the right of visit, search and seizure", not justifiable as self-defence, and an "unjustified interference with the rights of nations to navigate the seas and to trade freely with one another"; neither party could reasonably claim to be "actively a belligerent."
It called on Egypt to terminate restrictions on "the passage of international commercial shipping and goods" through the Canal, beyond what was needed for the safety of shipping in the Canal itself.
It was adopted at the 558th meeting by eight votes to none, the United States in favour, with China, India and the Soviet Union abstaining.

Egypt's case, as reconstructed by Leo Gross from the record, was that a state of belligerency with Israel still existed ("in the state of belligerency which in our opinion still exists between Egypt and Israel"), giving it wartime rights of visit, search and seizure of contraband on which its 1950 regulations rested; that the 1888 Constantinople Convention did not bind it toward Israel, a non-signatory; that the Security Council lacked authority over the matter; and that the restrictions guarded against sabotage.

At the 558th meeting Egypt's representative Mahmoud Fawzi said "Peace is acts and facts", described people driven from their homes, likened the Council's demand to an unconditional surrender, and reserved his government's rights.
Eban said the Council had rejected "one-sided belligerency or unilateral blockade" and affirmed the armistice as a path to permanent peace.

On 16 August 1951 Ecuador's representative argued that "there are at present no real hostilities", that self-defence could not be invoked without an actual armed attack, and that the interference could not be reconciled with the Constantinople Convention.

disputes.question: Could Egypt lawfully exercise belligerent rights against Israel-bound shipping after the 1949 armistice?

positions.view: Yes: a state of belligerency still existed, the armistice was not peace, the Constantinople Convention did not bind Egypt toward a non-signatory, and the Council lacked authority (Egypt's position as documented by Gross).

No: the armistice regime was permanent in character, no party could claim to be actively a belligerent, and the restrictions were an abuse of visit and search (Resolution 95; Israel and Ecuador in the Council).

entries.topic: Western defence schemes and Israel's place in them: the Robertson talks, the Middle East Command (1951), and Dulles's 1953 reassessment and the Jerusalem Foreign Ministry move

sources.label: Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", International Journal of Middle East Studies 36:4 (November 2004), pp. 657–673
FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 166: Editorial note on the Middle East Command approach to Egypt, October 1951
FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 82: Circular telegram 780.5/10–1951 on approaching Arab states and Israel about the MEC
FRUS 1951, vol. V, doc. 76: Acheson to the Embassy in Egypt, telegram 780.5/10–1651
FRUS 1952–54, vol. IX, doc. 54: Editorial note on Dulles's report on the Near East, 1 June 1953
Detroit Jewish News, 5 June 1953, report on Dulles's Near East address and testimony
US statement opposing the move of Israel's Foreign Ministry to Jerusalem, 28 July 1953 (text, Jewish Virtual Library)

claims.text: On 19 February 1951 General Sir Brian Robertson visited Israel; Sir William Strang had earlier floated a British base in Gaza with a corridor through Israel, or British bases in Israel under a treaty. Ben-Gurion called it "an insulting proposal" and asked instead that Israel be treated "as if they were Australia or New Zealand."
Herbert Morrison's reply of 23 April 1951 was lukewarm and offered only a back-door association with a regional defence body; Ben-Gurion insisted on full membership.

The United States, Britain and Turkey, joined by France, formally tendered to Egypt on 13 October 1951 an invitation to join a Middle East Command "as a founding member"; by 13 October Egypt had abrogated its 1936 treaty and the 1899 Sudan agreements with Britain, and it rejected the invitation on 15 October.
Acheson's note to Egypt called the abrogation "without validity" and a "serious retrograde step" for collective defence.

The State Department proposed that the four powers inform the Arab states (except Egypt) and Israel that they "intend establish MEC", without exhorting them to join; Israel was to receive a separate approach in Tel Aviv asking it to "give most serious consideration" to a question that "involves vitally" its security.

Shlaim writes that a British military delegation failed to break the deadlock in October 1952, that the Middle East Command idea faded in 1953, and that Israel's hope of military integration with the West faded with it.
On 1 June 1953 Secretary of State Dulles reported on his Near East trip over radio and television; the text is printed in the Department of State Bulletin, 15 June 1953, pp. 831–835.

As reported at the time, Dulles said the United States "should seek to allay the deep resentment against it that has resulted from the creation of Israel", that "Today the Arab peoples are afraid that the United States will back the new state of Israel in aggressive expansion", that Israel "should become a part of the Near East community", and that the US would stand by the Tripartite Declaration; he told the House Foreign Affairs Committee that policy toward Israel and the Arab states must be "impartial."

Dulles also said "the world religious community has claims in Jerusalem which take precedence over the political claims of any particular nation", and that some refugees "could be settled in the area presently controlled by Israel" while most could more readily be integrated into neighbouring Arab countries, depending on irrigation.

On 28 July 1953 the United States publicly regretted Israel's move of its Foreign Office from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, saying it would embarrass the UN, which "has a primary responsibility for determining the future status of Jerusalem", that it "will add to rather than to relax" tensions, and that the US would not move its embassy; the US had objected to the plan in July 1952 and March 1953.

entries.topic: The refugee question after Lausanne: UNRWA's first years, the Paris conference of 1951, the reintegration fund, and Palestinian political stirrings (1950–1953)

sources.label: Yearbook of the United Nations 1951–52, 'The Palestine Question' (excerpts, UNISPAL)
UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, Tenth Progress Report, A/1985 (23 January–19 November 1951)
General Assembly Resolution 513 (VI), 26 January 1952 (UNISPAL)
Truman, letter to committee chairmen on financing the UN Palestine refugee program, 27 July 1951 (Public Papers, Truman Library)
Jonathan Adler, "How plans to move Palestinians to Egypt backfired", New Lines Magazine, 12 May 2023
Yasir Arafat, Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question (PalQuest)
George Habash, Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question (PalQuest)
"Arab Nationalist Movement", Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict, via Encyclopedia.com

claims.text: UNRWA's first report (1 May 1950–30 June 1951) gives its headquarters as Beirut with five districts (Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Gaza and Israel), 133 international staff and 5,840 local staff; Director Howard Kennedy was succeeded by John B. Blandford Jr., who arrived on 4 July 1951.

Cash contributions to UNRWA in that period included the United States $27,450,000, Britain $6,200,000, France $2,285,714, Canada $894,313 and Israel $50,000; direct contributions in the region included Egypt $1,961,300, Iraq $980,000, Lebanon $457,800 and Jordan $323,900. Resolution 393 (V) had recommended $20 million for relief and $30 million for a reintegration fund for the year to 30 June 1952.

Truman told Congress on 27 July 1951 that the refugees' condition was "one of the principal causes of tension in the Near East" and that the Arab League had endorsed a large resettlement program for Palestinian refugees in Arab states.

The Conciliation Commission held a conference in Paris, at the Hôtel de Crillon, from 13 September to 19 November 1951, putting five proposals to the Arab delegations on 17 September and to Israel on 21 September: mutual cancellation of war-damage claims, Israeli repatriation of "a specified number of Arab refugees", a global compensation sum, mutual release of blocked accounts, and revision of the armistice agreements.

The Commission's Refugee Office valued abandoned Arab land at 100 million Palestine pounds (about $280 million at the then rate) and movable property at about £P20 million; the land covered 16,324 sq km, of which 4,574 sq km was cultivable.

Israel refused mutual cancellation of war damages on the ground that the Arab states were the aggressors, rejected repatriation because "major considerations of security and of political and economic stability made the return of Arab refugees impossible", offered compensation as a global sum that would end the refugee problem for Israel, and required that any settlement unfreeze Jewish accounts blocked in Iraq.

The Arab delegations said "there could be no limitations on the return of the refugees", that compensation should be individual, in cash and not tied to Israel's ability to pay, accepted the release of blocked accounts, and Syria said the armistice proposal sought to "ratify a fait accompli."

The Commission found that neither side showed "a willingness substantially to recede from its rigid position" and ended the conference on 19 November 1951; it recorded that Israel was not prepared to implement paragraph 11 of Resolution 194 (return) and the Arab governments were not prepared fully to implement paragraph 5 (peace negotiations), which had made it "impossible for the Commission to carry out its mandate."

Resolution 513 (VI) of 26 January 1952 endorsed a programme of $50 million for relief and $200 million for reintegration over about three years from 1 July 1951, "without prejudice to the provisions of paragraph 11 of resolution 194 (III)", with reintegration "either by repatriation or resettlement", and a 1952–53 budget of $118 million ($100 million for reintegration, $18 million for relief).

Jonathan Adler, working from Blandford's and Labouisse's papers, writes that UNRWA began working with Egypt on Sinai schemes in July 1950 and in June 1953 reserved $30 million of its $200 million reintegration fund for a siphon scheme to resettle 60,000 Gaza refugees on nearly 52,000 acres; Palestinians objected to it as a threat to the right of return.

Yasir Arafat, studying engineering in Cairo, took part in founding the Palestinian Students League in 1951 and was elected its president at the start of the 1952 academic year, holding the post until he graduated in 1956.

George Habash's family was expelled from Lydda after it fell on 11 July 1948; he graduated from the American University of Beirut in 1951, had been general secretary of the student society al-'Urwa al-Wuthqa in 1949–50, and in 1952 opened a free clinic for refugees and the poor in Amman with Wadi Haddad.

disputes.question: When was the Arab Nationalist Movement founded?

positions.view: At the beginning of the 1950s, at the American University of Beirut, by founders including George Habash and Hani al-Hindi.
Habash announced the movement at a general congress in Amman in December 1956, under the slogan 'Unity, Liberation, Revenge'.

disputes.question: What blocked a refugee settlement at Paris in 1951?

positions.view: Israel's position: return was impossible for reasons of security and of political and economic stability; the Arab states, as aggressors, should bear war damages; compensation would be a global sum ending Israel's responsibility.

The Arab position: there could be no limit on return, compensation must be individual and in cash, and armistice revision would ratify a fait accompli. The Commission found both sides unwilling to move.

entries.topic: Iran's oil nationalization and the Anglo-Iranian crisis, 1949–1952

sources.label: "Mossadeq and Oil Nationalization", Iran: A Country Study, Library of Congress Federal Research Division
International Court of Justice, Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. (United Kingdom v. Iran), case page
FRUS 1952–54, vol. X, doc. 41: Editorial note on the Harriman mission, July–September 1951
FRUS 1951–54, Iran (2nd ed.), doc. 121: Byroade to Acheson, 'Recommended Change in United States Policy Towards Iran', September 1952
"The Coup Against Iran's Mohammad Mossadegh", Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training oral histories (2015)
Time, "Challenge of the East" (Man of the Year), 7 January 1952 (text as reproduced)

claims.text: In 1949 the Majlis approved the First Development Plan (1948–55), to be financed largely from oil revenues, and the oil question dominated that year's elections; in November 1950 the Majlis oil committee, headed by Mossadeq, rejected a draft agreement with the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company that lacked fifty-fifty profit-sharing.

General Ali Razmara became prime minister in June 1950; the company offered fifty-fifty sharing in February 1951; in March 1951 Razmara, who had advised against nationalization, was assassinated by Khalil Tahmasebi of the Fadayan-e Islam.
On 15 March 1951 the Majlis voted to nationalize the oil industry, and in April 1951 the Shah, yielding to the Majlis and the street, named Mossadeq prime minister.

Britain filed a case at the International Court of Justice on 26 May 1951; the Court indicated provisional measures on 5 July 1951, and on 22 July 1952 decided that it had no jurisdiction, because Iran's 1932 declaration covered only disputes over treaties concluded after that date and the 1933 concession was not a treaty to which Britain was a party. Judges Alvarez, Hackworth, Read and Levi Carneiro dissented.

The Harriman mission left Washington on 13 July 1951 and reached Tehran on 15 July, met by an estimated 10,000 pro-Communist demonstrators outside the US Embassy; the British Stokes mission was in Tehran from 4 to 23 August, when the Anglo-Iranian talks were suspended.
In September 1951 Britain froze Iran's sterling assets and banned exports of goods to Iran.

In the summer of 1952 the Shah refused Mossadeq's demand to name the minister of war; Mossadeq resigned, three days of pro-Mossadeq rioting followed, and the Shah reappointed him; in August 1952 the Majlis granted him full powers for six months, later extended.

A US aide-mémoire of 31 July 1952 proposed "an immediate grant of $10 million to the Iranian Government" alongside British purchases of stored oil and arbitration on compensation; Truman and Churchill sent Mossadeq a joint message on 30 August 1952, which he first called "flatly unacceptable."

In September 1952 Assistant Secretary Byroade judged that "a nationalist government will neither bring in the communists nor fall victim to a communist revolt before next March", and recommended telling Britain that keeping Iran out of the communist world outweighed legal considerations, consulting US oil companies on buying 100,000–150,000 barrels a day, and telling Mossadeq that "the United States Government is not in the oil business."
In October 1952 Mossadeq cut diplomatic relations with Britain.
Time named Mossadeq its "Man of the Year" for 1951 in its issue of 7 January 1952, while describing him as "an appalling caricature of a statesman" and "the strange old wizard".

disputes.question: Did the International Court of Justice rule for Iran?

positions.view: The Library of Congress study says the Court found in Iran's favour.
The Court's own record shows that on 22 July 1952 it decided only that it had no jurisdiction to deal with the dispute; it did not rule on the merits.

entries.topic: TPAJAX and Boot: planning, approval, money, the August 1953 coup, and the 2013 and 2017 releases

sources.label: FRUS 1951–54, Iran (retrospective), doc. 363: CIA Directorate of Plans memorandum, 'Campaign to Install Pro-Western Government in Iran' (March 1954)
FRUS 1951–54, Iran (retrospective), doc. 225: Editorial note on the approval of the operational plan (June–July 1953)
National Security Archive, "CIA Confirms Role in 1953 Iran Coup", Electronic Briefing Book 435, 19 August 2013
Malcolm Byrne, "New documents about 1953 Iran coup enliven regime change debate", Atlantic Council IranSource, 13 July 2017
TPAJAX, Mary Ferrell Foundation cryptonym database (citing Wilber's 1954 CIA history, Risen in the New York Times 2000, and Gasiorowski)
"Mossadeq and Oil Nationalization", Iran: A Country Study, Library of Congress Federal Research Division
"1953 coup in Iran", Encyclopaedia Britannica (12 February 2024)
RFE/RL, "From the Archives" photo gallery on the 1953 coup (14 August 2013)
"The Coup Against Iran's Mohammad Mossadegh", Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training oral histories (2015)

claims.text: A CIA Directorate of Plans memorandum of March 1954 dates the project's inception to mid-May 1953 and records that it was approved by the President, the Secretary of State and the Director of Central Intelligence on 11 July 1953 under NSC 136/1, with two objectives: to bring about the fall of the Mossadeq government "through legal or quasi-legal methods" and to replace it with a pro-Western government under the Shah with Zahedi as prime minister.

The same memorandum says the President and the Secretary of State asked, before approving, for assurances that the British would be flexible on oil and that adequate US interim economic aid would go to the successor government.

It gives a grand total of $5,330,000 across three phases (operations to Zahedi's installation, follow-up to solidify the Shah and Zahedi, and emergency funds for the new government), with the amount of each phase still not declassified.

Wilber's 1954 CIA history records that the Director approved on 4 April 1953 a budget of $1,000,000 usable by the Tehran Station; James Risen's 2000 New York Times account reported that the CIA covertly funnelled $5 million to Zahedi's government two days after the coup, and Mark Gasiorowski that Zahedi and his colleagues received at least $50,000 beforehand.

FRUS notes that Kermit Roosevelt's memoir describes high-level approval at a State Department meeting on 25 June 1953, but no official record of that meeting has been found; a CIA chronology dates State Department and Foreign Office authorization to 11 July, a handwritten note says the DCI obtained presidential approval that day, and "No written authorization from the President has been found."

According to Malcolm Byrne's reading of the 2017 FRUS volume, Wilber's history confirms that Churchill approved the overthrow on 1 July 1953; after the failed first attempt of 14–15 August CIA headquarters advised Roosevelt to evacuate his team, but he stayed and, with Iranian collaborators, revived the operation; most operational cables for 16–19 August no longer exist, CIA officers having destroyed many records in the early 1960s.

On 3 August 1953 Mossadeq held a plebiscite on dissolving the Majlis and dissolved it; on 13 August the Shah appointed General Fazlollah Zahedi prime minister; Mossadeq refused to step down and arrested the Shah's emissary; the Shah fled; on 19 August pro-Shah army units and street crowds defeated Mossadeq's forces.

Afterwards Mossadeq was sentenced to three years' imprisonment and then kept under house arrest until his death in 1967; Foreign Minister Hosain Fatemi was executed; hundreds of National Front, Tudeh and other activists were arrested.
Britannica states that "Some 300 people died during fighting in Tehrān"; RFE/RL gives at least 300 dead in gun battles in Tehran.

On 19 August 2013 the National Security Archive posted 21 CIA items, including the internal history 'The Battle for Iran' with the TPAJAX name now restored, which "specifically states the agency planned and helped implement the coup" and is believed to be the CIA's first formal acknowledgement; Donald Wilber's 200-page history of March 1954 had been leaked to the New York Times in April 2000.

The State Department's 1989 FRUS volume on the period did not mention the US role; the historian Bruce Kuniholm called it "a fraud", the chair of the Historical Advisory Committee, Warren Cohen, resigned in 1990, and Congress passed a 1991 statute requiring a "thorough, accurate, and reliable documentary record"; British Foreign Office papers of 1978 show London seeking to keep material out, with a State Department official warning of "very embarrassing things about the British."

The retrospective FRUS volume of over 1,000 pages was released in June 2017; Byrne writes that the Obama administration had held it back over concern for the nuclear deal, that the Soviet threat dominates most of its reports, and that US analysts saw Ayatollah Kashani as a source of trouble and feared an "unholy alliance" with Mossadeq.

In oral histories, Lewis Hoffacker, third secretary in Tehran in 1951–53, said "our goal was to support the Shah and to try to contain Mossadegh"; John Stutesman recalled Ambassador Loy Henderson's "deep reluctance to have a covert operation displace a chief of state" (second-hand recollection).

disputes.question: When was the coup plan approved?

positions.view: June 1953: the Library of Congress study dates the Eisenhower administration's approval to June 1953, and Kermit Roosevelt's memoir describes approval at a 25 June meeting (no official record found).
11 July 1953: the CIA's March 1954 memorandum and its chronology date approval by the President, the Secretary of State and the DCI to 11 July; no written presidential authorization has been found.

disputes.question: Who carried out the coup, and why?

positions.view: It was a CIA-planned and -implemented operation with Britain; the CIA's own history says the agency planned and helped implement it.

Byrne notes that whether Americans and Britons or Iranians ultimately carried it out remains heavily disputed, as does the weight of Soviet fears against the commercial interests of the oil dispute; the documents are read both ways.

entries.topic: Iran and Israel before and after the coup: votes, de facto recognition, the consulate closed under Mossadeq, and the first economic links (1947–1953, with forward pointers)

sources.label: David Menashri, "Israel i. Relations with Iran", Encyclopaedia Iranica
Eitay Mack, "The unwritten history of Israel's alliance with the Shah's dictatorship", +972 Magazine, 24 June 2019

claims.text: Iran sat on the UN Special Committee on Palestine in 1947 as one of three members that opposed partition and favoured a federal solution, voted against partition on 29 November 1947, and voted against Israel's admission to the UN on 11 May 1949.
In the 1948 war Iran showed tacit solidarity with the Arab states but avoided combat and resisted Arab demands for direct military support.

In March 1949 Iran sent an unofficial envoy, Abbas Sayqal, to handle the claims of Iranian residents of Palestine; in 1949 it refused Israel's request to station a non-resident minister from Ankara in Tehran.

On 6 March 1950, while the Majlis was in recess, the government recognized Israel de facto without a formal announcement; Foreign Minister Entezam informed Abba Eban on 7 March, and Reza Safinia presented credentials as a "special envoy" on 26 March 1950.
Iran avoided official (de jure) recognition of Israel because of domestic and Arab pressure.
On 7 July 1951, shortly after Mossadeq took office, his government closed the Jerusalem consulate, citing "financial difficulties", without revoking de facto recognition.

On 11 June 1953, before the coup, the two countries' national banks signed an agreement opening a line of credit; in 1953 the Iranian–Israeli trading company IRIS was founded; Israel began buying Iranian oil in 1957 through foreign-flagged ships.

Menashri dates the first intelligence contact to September 1957, when General Teymur Bakhtiar, head of the newly established SAVAK, met Israel's ambassador Yaacov Zur in Paris and offered an exchange of intelligence; he dates Ben-Gurion's periphery concept to the late 1950s.
Eitay Mack writes that Israel's Foreign Ministry files on relations with Iran covering 1953 to 1979 have been declassified.

entries.topic: The Soviet turn: from patron to rupture — the Prague trial, the Doctors' Plot and the break of 1953

sources.label: Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", International Journal of Middle East Studies 36:4 (November 2004), pp. 657–673
"Rudolf Slánský", Encyclopaedia Britannica
JTA, "Prague trial throws Jews in Communist countries into mortal fear", 24 November 1952
"Doctors' Plot", Encyclopaedia Britannica
CIA Office of Current Intelligence, "The Doctors' Plot", working paper (Project CAESAR), 14 July 1953
"Soviet Embassy Bombed in Tel Aviv", Center for Israel Education timeline
"February 11 1953: Caught in a Cold War", The Jewish Chronicle archive feature

claims.text: Shlaim notes that in 1947 the United States and the Soviet Union both voted for partition, "one of rare occasions of agreement between them during the Cold War", that the Soviet Union extended recognition and that the Eastern bloc was Israel's main arms supplier in 1948; drawing on Uri Bialer he argues the Czech arms sales "continued for longer than would have been necessary" merely to create a Jewish state.

On 9 December 1949 Moscow voted for the internationalization of Jerusalem, marking a more critical Soviet line; according to Bialer, Soviet attitudes shifted further when Israel publicly backed the American position on Korea in 1950.

Rudolf Slánský, former general secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party, was arrested in November 1951; in November 1952 he and 13 others were tried and 11, including Slánský, were sentenced to death, among charges that he was a Zionist agent and a Western spy; most of those condemned were Jews. He was executed on 3 December 1952, cleared of the criminal charges in 1963 and restored to party membership in 1968.

The JTA reported that 12 of the 14 defendants were Jewish; that the indictment named Ben-Gurion and Sharett and described Israel's former minister to Czechoslovakia Ehud Avriel as "an American spy covered by the immunity of Israel diplomatic passports"; and that the alleged confessions of Mordecai Oren, a leader of Israel's left-wing Mapam party then under arrest in Czechoslovakia, were used to tie Israel to the case.
Shlaim describes the Prague show trial as denouncing Zionism and calling Israel an agent of American imperialism.

On 13 January 1953 Pravda and Izvestiya announced the arrest of nine doctors, at least six of them Jewish, accused of poisoning Andrei Zhdanov and Alexander Shcherbakov, plotting against Soviet marshals, and working for US and British intelligence and "the interests of international Jewry."

A CIA working paper of 14 July 1953 says the announcement tied the doctors to a "Jewish-bourgeois nationalist group" backed by American and British intelligence, notes the affair's "clearly antiSemitic overtones", and records New Times on 21 January calling Zionists and Israeli officials the "executors of a US State Department spy ring in the USSR."
On 19 January 1953 Sharett condemned Soviet antisemitic and anti-democratic practices in the Knesset.

On 9 February 1953 a bomb of about 70 pounds of explosives went off in the garden of the Soviet legation in Tel Aviv, injuring one Soviet diplomat and the wives of two others; it was blamed on a group known as the Tzrifin Underground, whose leader Yaakov Heruti denied involvement, and the government lacked proof.

Soviet Foreign Minister Vyshinsky summoned Israel's minister Samuel Eliashiv at 1 a.m. and handed him a note demanding that the legation's diplomats "leave Moscow without delay", citing the "terrorist act"; the Jewish Chronicle dates the break to 11 February 1953, and Shlaim says Moscow broke relations that day despite Israel's official apology.

Stalin died on 5 March 1953, before any trial; in April 1953 Pravda announced that the charges against the doctors were false and the confessions obtained by torture, and the surviving doctors were exonerated.
Relations were restored in July 1953 after Israel said it would not join any alliance against the Soviet Union; the Center for Israel Education gives the announcement date as 21 July 1953.
Interpretation (Shlaim): the rift was "probably beyond repair", and by the end of 1953 non-identification had been "replaced by an explicit pro-Western position."

positions.view: Moscow: Soviet policy followed its own 'developmental logic' (Sharett), shown in the Prague trial and the Doctors' Plot; this was the Israeli establishment's view.

Partly Israel's own alignment: Soviet aid and goodwill were tied to Israel's foreign-policy orientation more than assumed, and cooled as Israel sided with the West on Korea (Bialer, as cited by Shlaim).

entries.topic: "Under God": the Knights of Columbus campaign (1951–1953) and the 1954 change, in its Cold War and domestic frames

sources.label: Gene T. Janikowski (Knights of Columbus South Carolina State Council), "How the words 'under God' came to be added to the Pledge of Allegiance"
Congressional Record, Extensions of Remarks, 17 October 2002, p. E1900 (history of 'under God')
US Solicitor General, brief on the merits, Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow (2003–04), quoting H.R. Rep. No. 1693 and S. Rep. No. 1287 (83rd Cong., 1954)
NPR, "How 'One Nation' Didn't Become 'Under God' Until The '50s Religious Revival" (interview with Kevin Kruse), 30 March 2015

claims.text: On 22 April 1951 the Knights of Columbus Board of Directors adopted a resolution adding "under God" to the Pledge as recited at its Fourth Degree assemblies.

In 1952 Knights of Columbus state councils in Florida, South Dakota, New York and Michigan urged Congress to amend the Pledge, and on 21 August 1952 the Supreme Council urged that the change be made general.
On 20 August 1953 the Supreme Council repeated its call and sent copies to the President, the Vice President, the Speaker and every member of Congress; seventeen House resolutions followed.

Representative Louis C. Rabaut of Michigan's resolution passed both houses, and President Eisenhower signed the change on Flag Day, 14 June 1954; on the House floor Rabaut said "From their earliest childhood our children must know" what "under God" means.

The House report (H.R. Rep. No. 1693, 1954) presented the words as rejecting the communist philosophy "with its attendant subservience of the individual"; the Senate report (S. Rep. No. 1287) said: "The spiritual bankruptcy of the Communists is one of our strongest weapons in the struggle for men's minds."

Eisenhower wrote to Supreme Knight Luke Hart on 17 August 1954 that he was "particularly thankful to you for your part in the movement", and said the words would remind Americans "that despite our great physical strength we must remain humble."

Kevin Kruse traces an earlier campaign, Rev. James Fifield's Spiritual Mobilization, funded by business leaders including J. Howard Pew and Alfred Sloan, with about 17,000 minister representatives and the slogan "Freedom Under God", including a July 4, 1951 ceremony organized by Cecil B. DeMille.

Kruse says the Knights' proposal at first "doesn't go anywhere" and "catches fire" only after Eisenhower's own pastor endorsed it; "In God we trust" went onto a stamp in 1954, onto paper money by act of Congress in 1955, and became the national motto in 1956.

Interpretation (Kruse): the common story that "the Soviet Union discovered the bomb and the United States rediscovered God" papers over domestic conflict; the architects of this language were most worried about the New Deal and Fair Deal administrations.

disputes.question: What motive drove 'under God' into the Pledge?

positions.view: The Cold War contrast with atheistic communism, as stated in the 1954 House and Senate reports.
A longer domestic campaign by business-funded clergy against the New Deal, of which the Cold War framing was a later layer (Kruse).

disputes.question: In which year did the National Fraternal Congress in Boston adopt its resolution (24 September)?

positions.view: 1952 (Congressional Record, 2002).
1953 (Janikowski, whose chronology is internally inconsistent).
